results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response:
The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004952 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. The calyx is the part of the mushroom body closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents. The pedunculus is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes. The mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages. 

VFB holds extensive data related to the mushroom body, including 602 neurons with some part in the mushroom body, 176 parts of the mushroom body, and over 22,000 images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body.

results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response:
The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells, including alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells. These types are further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes. Specifically, gamma Kenyon cells are known to exist and innervate only the gamma lobe in the adult. VFB holds detailed information on gamma Kenyon cells, including images, subclasses, expression patterns, scRNAseq data, and transgene expression.

results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The LPLC2 visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer. Its dendrites extend outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, allowing it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli. LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. It has connections to various neurons, including adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, and transmedullary neurons. The activity of LPLC2 elicits a jump escape response. 
Available VFB data includes information on 2,548 neuron types, including the LPLC2, which has a unique ID of [1813403998](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open 1813403998 in Virtual Fly Brain") (VFB_jrch0fva).

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The giant fiber neuron is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior (Thomas and Wyman, 1984). It has a distinct anatomy, with a large descending axon that arborizes in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. There is one giant fiber neuron per hemisphere, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum (Koto et al., 1981). The giant fiber neuron can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective (Koto et al., 1981; Power, 1948).

VFB holds extensive data on the giant fiber neuron, including 22 images, 14 records of transgene expression, 361 downstream connectivity classes, and 435 upstream connectivity classes. For example, the expression pattern of P{VT046265-GAL4} in the giant fiber neuron is available. 

Relevant publications on the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Sturner et al. (2025), which provide information on its anatomy, connectivity, and role in jump escape behavior. 

Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron, such as P{VT046265-GAL4}, are also available, allowing for targeted manipulation and study of this neuron. 

Overall, the giant fiber neuron is a well-characterized neuron with a unique anatomy and connectivity, and its study has contributed significantly to our understanding of jump escape behavior in Drosophila.
